opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, and honestly my view has shifted quite a bit.

A few years ago, I saw research and entrepreneurship as two different worlds. Research was about curiosity: you chase a question because it's interesting, you publish, and the community decides whether it matters. Entrepreneurship seemed like the opposite. You take something that already works and spend your energy on products, markets, fundraising, execution. I think many people in academia still see it that way, and I used to feel there was something slightly impure about mixing them.

What changed is that in AI, especially in the last few years, the line between doing frontier research and building something real has almost disappeared. The most important research questions now, like how models understand the visual world, how they reason, and how they connect to the physical world, can't really be answered with a few GPUs and a paper deadline. You need scale, sustained engineering, data infrastructure, and a team that works toward one goal for years. That looks a lot like a company.

So I now think of entrepreneurship as another way of doing research, sometimes the only way to pursue certain ideas seriously. A startup can be a vehicle for a research conviction. If you believe strongly in a direction that the big labs aren't prioritizing, building your own organization around it is one of the few ways to test it properly.

I've also become more humble about what entrepreneurship demands. Being a good researcher doesn't make you a good founder. You have to care about people, about how a team grows, and about making decisions with incomplete information, which is uncomfortable for researchers who are trained to wait until the evidence is clean. I've learned that taste, judging which problems are worth solving, matters in both worlds. In a company, though, you pay for bad taste much more directly.

Overall, I've gone from seeing them as a trade-off to seeing them as complementary. The best research environments borrow a founder's urgency and ownership, and the best AI companies, at least the ones I admire, keep a researcher's curiosity and willingness to be wrong. I'm still figuring out the balance, but I no longer see choosing one as giving up the other.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he previously viewed research and entrepreneurship as separate, but now sees entrepreneurship as another way to do research and considers them complementary.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because my answer today is quite different from what it would have been even three or four years ago.

When I was at FAIR, and honestly for most of my career, I had a fairly clean mental model: research and entrepreneurship were two separate tracks. Research was about asking questions nobody had asked yet, publishing, pushing the frontier, and being okay with most ideas failing. Entrepreneurship was about picking something that already worked and scaling it, finding product-market fit, raising money. I respected people who did the second thing, but I didn't think of it as something I was doing, or should be doing.

What changed is that the gap between those two activities collapsed. In the last few years, the time from a research idea to something people actually use went from maybe five or ten years down to months, sometimes weeks. When ConvNeXt or the DiT work came out, I watched them show up in production systems almost immediately. That forces you to confront the fact that the research you choose to do is already a kind of bet about the world, in the same way a startup is a bet. You're allocating scarce attention and compute to one direction instead of another, and you're implicitly saying, "I think this matters more than that." That's a founder's decision, whether or not you call it that.

The second thing I came to appreciate, especially after moving to NYU and running my own group, is that a lab is a small company in almost every way that matters. You have to recruit, you have to find resources, you have to set a direction that's ambitious but not suicidal, and you have to be honest with yourself when something isn't working. The main difference is the objective function. A company optimizes for survival and growth. A lab optimizes for being right about something important before anyone else is. Those overlap more than people think, but they aren't identical, and I think a lot of the tension you see in the field right now comes from people confusing one for the other.

And that leads to the thing I feel most strongly about now. I used to think the pressure from industry was mostly a threat to academic research, that it would pull all the talent and compute away and leave universities doing toy problems. I still worry about that. But I've also come to believe that the most valuable role for academic research right now is to be contrarian in a disciplined way. When the whole industry converges on scaling the same recipe, the real opportunity, scientifically and even commercially, is in asking the questions that don't fit the roadmap. Why do these representations work? What are we missing about visual understanding that language-first models paper over? Those questions are hard to justify inside a company on a quarterly timeline, but they're exactly where the next big shift is going to come from.

So if I had to summarize how my view changed: I used to see entrepreneurship as what you do after research. Now I see them as the same core skill, which is deciding what's worth betting on under uncertainty, just with different time horizons and different definitions of success. And I've become much more comfortable saying that a research group should think like founders about direction, while refusing to think like founders about what counts as a result.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Xie now sees entrepreneurship and research as “the same core skill,” while noting different time horizons and definitions of success. It does not clearly state that he has come to see entrepreneurship as distinct from research.

astra-6.text:
I used to see research and entrepreneurship as fairly separate paths. Research was about finding an interesting problem and developing a new idea; entrepreneurship was about taking an idea and turning it into a product. Over the past few years, I’ve started to see that boundary as much less clear.

Both involve making decisions under uncertainty. You have to develop conviction about something before you have enough evidence to know that it will work. But entrepreneurship adds a different kind of discipline: an idea can be intellectually interesting, and even technically successful, without solving a problem that people actually care about.

So the question for me has shifted from simply, “Can we make this work?” to, “If we make this work, what does it enable, and who does it help?” That doesn’t mean every research project should become a company. Research needs room for exploration. But I increasingly see entrepreneurship as a way to carry a research vision further—to build the team and the feedback loop needed to turn a possibility into something people can use.

r001.rationale: The response says the boundary between research and entrepreneurship has become much less clear and describes entrepreneurship as carrying a research vision further. It notes differences in discipline, but does not clearly state that Xie has come to see entrepreneurship as distinct from research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I used to see research and entrepreneurship as fairly separate paths. Research was about finding something new, and entrepreneurship was about turning something into a product. Over the past few years, I’ve started to see more overlap between them.

In both cases, you’re working with uncertainty. You have to decide which problem matters, form a hypothesis, and then learn from what actually happens. A beautiful idea isn’t enough by itself. In research, you need evidence that it works; in a company, you need evidence that it solves a real problem for someone.

But the feedback is different. As a researcher, you can become very focused on what other researchers find interesting. Building something forces you to ask: Who needs this? What would make them use it? Those questions can actually lead to better research questions.

So I’ve become less attached to the distinction. What interests me is whether there’s an important problem and whether we can build the right team to make progress on it. Sometimes that fits best within a research lab, and sometimes it might require a company.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he used to see research and entrepreneurship as separate, but over time came to see more overlap and became less attached to the distinction. It does not state that he has come to see entrepreneurship as distinct from research.
